section.title: Sergey Levine: Robot Generalization, Data Flywheels, and Humanoid Timelines
section.deck: Levine argues that humanoid progress depends on generalization, diverse data and a healthy ecosystem, and gives a rough timeline of single-digit years for structured deployments.

blocks.text: Levine, speaking about work at Physical Intelligence, argues that humanoid robotics is still finding its fundamental technologies. It has not yet reached the predictable scaling stage that drove language models. Demos are informative, but they often hide how little generalization they show. Levine's central claim is that robots improve through diverse, autonomous experience inside a healthy ecosystem of data, hardware and manufacturing. The timeline Levine gives is single-digit years for structured deployments and a few years more for less structured ones, though Levine calls the forecast hard.
blocks.heading: Levine's view: generalization and ecosystem health matter more than demos

blocks.question: Where is humanoid robotics today, and how will the technology be deployed?
answer: Levine says machine learning works at scale, but only if the right thing is scaled. Transformers mattered because they scaled better than the earlier LSTM designs, not because they were mathematically elegant. Technology moves in phases: first find a scalable design, then put industrial-scale effort into data and model size. Levine says robotics is not yet at the GPT-4-to-GPT-5 stage of that effort, so progress will not follow a predictable monthly curve. The puzzle pieces are falling into place, but the scaling coefficients are hard to forecast.
blocks.speaker: Sergey Levine

blocks.question: What are the most astonishing emerging capabilities you have seen so far?
answer: Levine recalls that in late 2024 a laundry policy pulled two shirts from the hamper at once. It set one aside, disentangled the pair and folded the other. Levine says nobody watching the evaluation expected that, and that it looked like common sense, even if training data may explain it.

Levine finds recent mistakes more revealing. In a kitchen evaluation, a robot that could not open the expected drawer put the utensils into the oven beside it. In a dishwashing test, the robot tracked cleaned plates on a scratch-pad memory. It dropped one, then moved its base so the dropped plate was out of view. Levine says these errors resemble a child's mistakes, and that the robot still needs to grow up.
blocks.speaker: Sergey Levine

blocks.question: Among Figure, Tesla and other humanoid efforts, has any achievement impressed you?
answer: Levine says the most inspiring development is the takeoff of autonomous driving. Robotics is often criticized as always the technology of the future, like nuclear fusion, but people said the same about driving. Levine notes that a Waymo in San Francisco now takes riders with no driver. Levine says this is no accident in the mid-2020s, as large-scale machine learning pieces fit real physical systems. Driving and manipulation differ, but the example shows that learning-based technology can work in the physical world.
blocks.speaker: Sergey Levine

blocks.question: If a major AI lab such as Anthropic invested heavily in robotics, how would the industry change, and would competitors worry?
answer: Levine says robotics is a less healthy ecosystem than computer vision or language. Those fields have freely available data, wide acceptance of learning, and fewer concerns about physical harm. Levine notes that robotics has not traditionally shared data, and that safety concerns there are not the same as a device causing physical harm.

Levine says more learning-based activity would shift thinking toward learned controllers and shared data. Levine is proud of the work at Physical Intelligence, but argues that it will take more than one company to change how everyone thinks about the field.
blocks.speaker: Sergey Levine

blocks.question: Chinese robotics demonstrations look impressive from outside. Are Chinese labs further along, and what is the lesson?
answer: Levine says the useful lesson for US and European researchers is that robotics needs a healthy ecosystem across all its parts. That means strong researchers, open source, and healthy supply chains, manufacturing and hardware R&D, not only computer science and model building. Levine says the United States does some of these well and has let others slip.

Levine suggests studying strong results from labs anywhere, then investing across every facet. Levine disclaims business and investment expertise, so does not claim to know how to do this. Levine argues the field is holistic and cannot be outsourced one piece at a time.

followups.question: As a robotics researcher in the US, what would most improve the field?
answer: Levine says reliable, low-cost hardware is a big deal. Much research hardware now comes from China. Levine describes it as inexpensive, high quality and meeting the standards researchers generally need. Levine says it would be good to source that hardware domestically too, and does not think that is impossible.
followups.speaker: Sergey Levine

blocks.speaker: Sergey Levine

blocks.question: Will the first lab to reach scale pull ahead through a deployment flywheel, whether in the US or China?
answer: Levine says there is much truth to the flywheel, but the lab must scale the right thing. The better framing is a positive feedback loop in which more deployed robots mean more model capability. A welding robot on a car assembly line may make many welds each month, yet that data alone is unlikely to produce anything more capable than a welding robot.
Levine argues that data is not a fungible commodity like oil or electricity. It has to be diverse, and is more like “an education program for your robot” than a commodity.

followups.question: When do you first expect that flywheel to appear in the world?
answer: Levine says the timing depends on how much structure developers accept. Unstructured home deployment brings diverse data at once, but the safety bar is high because people are present. More structured tasks face fewer safety issues and are more predictable, but each new data point carries less variety. Levine describes a trade-off between starting earlier on a smaller slope and starting later on a larger one.
Levine's sense is single-digit years rather than double-digit years. Structured tasks may arrive now or next year, and less structured ones a few more years out, but probably not a decade.
followups.speaker: Sergey Levine

blocks.speaker: Sergey Levine

blocks.question: Could you sketch milestones on a roadmap toward a robot in the home?
answer: Levine warns that a demonstration often hides the level of generalization. Generalization is a property of many trials, not one. A mundane task with an unseen object in an untested room can be harder than a rehearsed backflip. So the roadmap centers on better generalization and on a mechanism that improves it with experience.

One milestone is a concrete system that improves through autonomous experience in a setting it was not trained for. It should reach practical robustness rather than capping out near 50 percent. Another is transferring common sense so a robot can recover from surprises. Levine uses the driver's instinct to slow down for a fire truck or traffic cones, even in an unfamiliar situation, as the example.
blocks.speaker: Sergey Levine

blocks.question: Are you less interested in a narrow humanoid doing one assembly-line step, since that is not a step toward general intelligence?
answer: Levine says narrow work is not uninteresting. The real world has leaky abstractions that make even narrow tasks more complex than they seem. Autonomous driving shows this. Early plans to use magnetic sensors along highways and transmitters in cars failed, because messy exceptions broke the system in the 1 percent of cases that matter. What worked was facing the mess in San Francisco.

Levine expects robotic manipulation to follow the same path. Leaving a fully structured factory means facing the full scope of the problem, even when most of the time the task looks straightforward. Levine adds that recovering from a spatula placed in an oven shows common sense can help a robot fix its own mistakes.
blocks.speaker: Sergey Levine

blocks.question: Does Figure's live-streamed package-sorting demo show generalization?
answer: Levine thinks it does, and welcomes the creative ways people are making generalization visible, such as live demos and long time-lapses.

Levine describes Physical Intelligence's long-horizon runs. One robot assembled boxes at a chocolate factory over several days. Another made espresso drinks for 13 hours, cleaning up spilled grounds along the way. Levine jokes that the main downside was staff losing sleep to caffeine.

followups.question: Did the robot clean up its spills by itself?
answer: Not entirely. A person issued high-level prompts about every five minutes, including commands to clean the machine. Levine says that could be automated in principle, and the team is working on the high-level policy that issues those commands. Levine adds, with a laugh, that the robot also had to be told to clean up before the next drink.
followups.speaker: Sergey Levine

blocks.speaker: Sergey Levine

blocks.question: What is the best robot training data, what is the worst, and what are the trade-offs between simulated and physical interaction data?
answer: Levine says data is easier for a model to absorb when it is grounded in physical understanding. A pilot learns in a flight simulator because they know it abstracts a real aircraft. A person watching someone cook can file away an add-salt step without copying every movement. Levine argues that a robot foundation model trained on lots of real embodied data may absorb other sources better.

That reverses a common instinct from LLMs, which is to start with internet video and add robot data on top. Levine says the evidence points the other way. A colleague and a Georgia Tech collaborator found that, with a small model and little robot data, human and robot experience stayed fully separate in the internal representations. With lots of robot data from many robots, features grouped by task instead. At full robot-data scale, the human and robot embeddings lined up perfectly, which Levine sees as a strong sign that a solid robot base absorbs other data well.
blocks.speaker: Sergey Levine

blocks.question: Does the base model need data from the exact robot it will run on, and can skills transfer between robots?
answer: Levine says cross-embodiment models are a major focus, but deployment still generally needs data from the target robot. The better measure of generalization is how little experience a new robot needs to borrow skills from others. The model needs surprisingly little special machinery. There is no factorized representation for different morphologies. It outputs one large vector, padded with zeros when a robot has fewer degrees of freedom, and trains on all robots together.

Levine says transfer works best through the right intermediate representation. Text thinking carries high-level structure, such as opening a drawer before putting away silverware. Image thinking can carry low-level skill. The model dreamed up the next milestone as an image, which let a UR5 arm fold a shirt without any shirt-folding data for that arm. Imagining a folded shirt is easier than getting joint angles right.

followups.question: So the model outputs an image of what its video sensor should see next?
answer: Levine says it is like image editing, and video prediction could work too. The key is imagining progress on the task. Some planning is semantic and some is spatial, as when a rock climber pictures the arm reaching for the next hold.
followups.speaker: Sergey Levine

blocks.speaker: Sergey Levine

blocks.question: What would make you say single-digit years is coming, rather than a long tail with policy challenges?
answer: Levine says a key difference is how thin the robot's software stack is. Training the foundation model is hard, because data must be gathered, curated and labelled. The software on the robot is very simple by comparison. Counted in lines of code, it is much smaller than a traditional autonomous vehicle stack, which started earlier with older technology and evolved over years.

Levine says safety is real and probably among the harder parts of the problem, but it is less of a hard stop. Dropping a fragile object is far less bad than a car hitting someone. Developers can pick tasks, environments and hardware where problems are milder. Levine argues that a simpler stack plus milder challenges make deployment easier, and that early deployment feeds a flywheel.
blocks.speaker: Sergey Levine

blocks.question: If humanoid robotics did not succeed in single-digit years, what would be the most likely reason?
answer: Levine says it would come down to reliability. Robots need more robustness and generalization than people expect from LLMs and image tools. Those tools are interactive: a user can rephrase and iterate. A robot delivers its full value only when it acts autonomously, so needing someone to iterate on every task defeats the purpose. Demos can also mislead about how close a system is to practical robustness.

Levine believes in reinforcement learning that uses autonomous experience to fine-tune the last few percentage points, from about 95 to 100 percent, but says that is not yet solved. If progress takes longer, Levine says it would be because the bar is higher. Levine does not favor discarding foundation-model methods, since the puzzle pieces are good, but the methods need more work to cross the robustness threshold.
blocks.speaker: Sergey Levine

blocks.question: In LLMs everyone seems to do similar things. Is robotics the same, or are there hot-take architectures?
answer: Levine says robotics is more varied than it looks. The dividing line is between embracing the foundation-model approach and building specialized vertical systems. The principle is that a general model trained on many problems beats a narrow specialist on one problem. Levine uses machine translation as the example: a general language model can outperform a dedicated translation system.

Levine says this is uncomfortable in robotics. A warehouse team may find it strange to collect data on putting away silverware in kitchens. Yet breadth of data builds generalizable skills that a well-built model can repurpose, even for warehouse edge cases. Levine says this cuts against the traditional approach of building vertically integrated robotic systems.
blocks.speaker: Sergey Levine

blocks.question: If AI companies become wildly successful, what safety and government concerns come up, and how would you handle them for a generalist robot model?
answer: Levine says AI safety is not new. Stuart Russell, a colleague at UC Berkeley, was raising these issues more than a decade ago. Technology moves so fast that the important questions depend on how society reacts and which tools get adopted. Those are hard to anticipate. Levine has no fully satisfying answer. The approach is empirical: release systems, see what goes right and wrong in the real world, and adjust.

Levine argues that if computer-only AI already raises concerns, systems that can do everything people can physically do will raise strictly more. The risks are real, so the work is to keep watching and adjust.
blocks.speaker: Sergey Levine

blocks.question: If everything goes well and robots are very capable in ten years, is the north star the end of human labor?
answer: Levine says it is a mistake to think of robots as mechanical people. Personal computing did not replace brains. Computers spread into desks, pockets, refrigerators and cars. Levine suggests physical actuation could appear in many everyday things, so people still do many tasks but get help with them.

Coding agents are a closer example. Levine says the endgame is unclear, but software engineers Levine has spoken with mostly find agents empowering rather than alarming, because they amplify how much work one person can do. Levine calls it a real job where AI adds leverage, though the outcome remains to be seen.
blocks.speaker: Sergey Levine

blocks.question: Are there a few top papers that show the breakthroughs people should know about in humanoid robotics?
answer: Levine offers a partly self-promoting pick: the ACT paper, which Levine also calls the ALOHA paper. Levine is a co-author, and says almost all the work was done by lead author Tony. The ideas were not new, but they were illustrated well. Low-cost hobbyist arms, which Levine says cost about $7,000 each, used a leader-follower teleoperation rig to collect data for very dexterous tasks. A fairly simple transformer-based model could perform many of them.

Levine says the insight is to put the right pieces together and trust what a simple robot can do with a good learning system. The code was open sourced and is the starter kit many people use. Levine recommends the paper to newcomers, because the details matter even if they need not be complicated.
blocks.speaker: Sergey Levine

blocks.question: Boston Dynamics once had striking demonstrations and much mindshare, but you hear less about them now. Is there an industry shift behind that?
answer: Levine says robotics is about building complex systems, from wiring and power sources to actuators and high-level planning. Classic Boston Dynamics results show sophisticated, carefully designed hardware, with traditional control by skilled engineers and less emphasis on decision making. That made sense when the physical body was the bottleneck. Now, Levine says, hardware is often good enough, and the big challenge is a decision loop that reacts intelligently to the environment.

Levine draws the line between controls and AI. Controls handle the robot's own body, such as a backflip on flat ground. AI must account for the world, such as picking up a coffee cup. Levine also says a hand-designed controller proves a skill is possible and often simple enough to learn, so the skill can be automated without controls engineers in the loop.
blocks.speaker: Sergey Levine

blocks.question: Knowing what you know now, what would you tell yourself when you first entered the field?
answer: Levine says the main change is recognizing that robotics needs broad prior knowledge. Levine once shared the common idea that robots should learn from scratch, as people do. The arm farm project at Google had many arms grasp millions of objects in a conference room. The arms learned to grasp, but that was a poor stepping stone to more complex skills.

Levine says language itself was not the point. Prior knowledge used as a scaffold is the point. Humans and monkeys absorb much of their knowledge through observation rather than language. Without prior knowledge, a robot faces a harder problem than humans do, like assembling flat-pack furniture without ever having seen any. Levine's advice to a younger self is to take prior knowledge more seriously, while still valuing learning from experience.
blocks.speaker: Sergey Levine
